latin.86: VI. Sed fortasse illa tandem aliquando emerget ex verf. 19. Sicut per unius inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi, ita per unius obedientiam justi constituentur multi: Nullo certe modo. Argumentatur ex eo D. G. non uno modo, & primo quidem sic. Idem Apostolus agit hoc versu quod reliquis illis diffusiùs prosecutus fuerat. Atqui hoc versu manifeste agit de imputatione. Ergo & de eadem imputatione superiora intelligenda sunt. Respondeo ad minorem, Apostolum hoc versu non agere de imputatione: aut si agit de imputatione, non agere de imputatione immediata seu antecedente, quam solam nego. Nam si idem agit hoc versu quod in superioribus, in quibus de ista imputatione eum non egisse patuit, consequens est, eum de ista imputatione non agere in isto versu.
latin.87: Deinde, inquit, vix disertius & efficaciùs poterat Apostolus imputationem Adamici peccati significare, quam factum est his verbis, claram oppositionem continentibus inter Adami inobedientiam, & obedientiam Christi. Qui factum est igitur, ut maximi viri versum illum exponentes, imputationem illam in Apostoli verbis non animadverterint, sed rejecerint potius? verum pergat, Obedientiam Christi actualem significat, qua Christus factus est obediens Patri usque ad mortem crucis, Phil. 2.8. Ergo & obedientiam Adami actualem, qua Dei mandatum violavit: ut mirum sit qua ratione neget Vir doctus hic παρακοῆς voce ab Apostolo designari peccatum Adami actuale. Nam quod addit, non designari peccatum actuale praecisum à corruptione, quam in Adamo peperit, hoc parum moramur. Quid, affirmare voce παρακοῆς solum peccatum Adami significari, non quidem actuale praecisum ab habituali, sed simul cum habituali, quae sunt Placei verba, estne negare, ea voce designari peccatum Adami actuale?
latin.88: Cur vero id non moratur? Etenim, inquit, sive praecisum ab illa corruptione, sive conjunctum cum ea, semper tamen designari intelligitur, quod ad causam nostram satis est. Immo vero si causam defendis imputationis immediatae, id non satis est. oportet enim sic imputari peccatum actuale praecisum à corruptione, siquidem haec est illius imputati poena proprie dicta. non potest enim idem peccatum esse poena sui ipsius, praesertim poena proprie dicta.
latin.89: Hinc duplex argumentum se posse putat colligere: primum ex vi oppositionis. Eadem ratione constituimur peccatores in Adamo, qua justi constituimur in Christo. Atqui in Christo justi constituimur per justitiae ipsius imputationem. Ergo & peccatores in Adamo per peccati ipsius imputationem. Etsi nobis conclusio non nocet imputationem mediatam agnoscentibus, tamen major propositio falsa est. In eo enim ipso, de quo agitur, discrimen observatum est à viris maximis, uti patuit ex superioribus nostris responsionibus. Constituti enim sumus peccatores propagato in nos peccato inhaerente quod meretur mortem, non sumus constituti justi justitia inhaerente quae mereatur vitam.
latin.90: Deinde, inquit, ex verbis per inobedientiam Adae peccatores constituimur. Nam per actualem alterius inobedientiam constitui non possumus peccatores, nisi imputative; quia quod alterius est personaliter, nostrum fieri nequit, neque nos inde denominari, nisi imputationis interventu. Atqui per actualem Adami inobedientiam constituimur peccatores. Ergo imputative. Quid est negare propagationem peccati inhaerentis, si hoc non est?
latin.91: Audiamus ergo potius ejus Antecessorem Chamierum, Illud etiam non omittendum: per unius inobedientiam multos esse constitutos peccatores ἁμαρτωλούς; quod vocabulum in Scripturis sumitur pro iis in quibus est re vera peccatum contrarium legi Dei. Et paulo post. Uno verbo. Nunquam ἁμαρτωλὸς dicitur de simplici reatu, & absque ullo vitio aut peccato. Ergo, cum dixit Paulus multos esse constitutos peccatores per unius inobedientiam: NIHIL ALIUD intellexit, nisi eo Adami peccato effectum esse, ut omnes homines re vera, & in se se peccatores essent. Et alio loco, A Paulo autem doceri unicum esse numero in omnibus peccatum originale, hoc vero insigniter falsum. Nam contra. Per unius inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi. Eodem capite. Peccator autem est, qui ipse habet peccatum suum: non autem cui alienum imputatur. Et rursus. In Adamo peccavimus omnes: quia Adamus primus peccavit: & inde initium factum peccati in omnibus hominibus: at in nobis etiam peccamus: quia ejus peccato constituti sumus peccatores: id est, ab eo in nos peccatum propagatum. Et illius inobedientia eodem modo sumus omnes constituti peccatores: quo nostra etiam propria jam vere sumus peccatores: alioqui falsum esset, nos illius inobedientia constitutos esse peccatores. Alio loco ait nos per inobedientiam Adami constitutos esse peccatores, non formaliter, sed causaliter, quia est causa efficiens qualitatis illius per quam sumus formaliter peccatores: Sicut, inquit, podagrici causa est parens podagricus, sive podagra in parente: quae tamen non est podagra filii. Audiamus etiam Petrum Martyrem contra argumentantem. Hic, inquit, annotabimus, cum Apostolus dicit, Per unius inobedientiam peccatores multos esse constitutos, ex his verbis argumentum haberi adversus eos, qui putant peccatum originis non esse cuique proprium: sed unum tantum extitisse, illudque fuisse in Adamo, quo nos nexi, obligati sumus ad mortem & damnationem. Quum enim dicantur peccatores constituti, oportet, ut ipsi aut peccatum habeant, aut saltem habuerint. Nam alieno vitio nemo dicitur peccator.

pass_a.86: Head VI begins. Placeus asks whether the contested thesis finally appears from Romans 5:19, quoting the parallel: through one person's disobedience many were made sinners, and through one person's obedience many will be made righteous. Answer first: no, not at all. Opponent D. Garissoles (D. G.) builds more than one proof from the verse. Proof one runs: in this verse Paul is still doing the work he developed at greater length in the preceding verses; and here he obviously discusses imputation; so those preceding verses must also concern that same imputation. Placeus targets the middle claim (the minor). Either Paul is not discussing imputation in this verse at all, or, if imputation is in view, it is not the immediate / prior-to-corruption kind — and that is the only kind Placeus refuses. Chain: if verse 19 merely continues the earlier verses, and those earlier verses already showed Paul was not teaching that refused kind of imputation, then verse 19 does not teach it either.
pass_a.87: Garissoles's next move: Paul could hardly have pointed more plainly or strongly to the imputation of Adam's sin than by these words, which set Adam's disobedience cleanly against Christ's obedience. Placeus's counter-question: why then did the leading expositors of the verse fail to find that imputation in Paul's wording, and even push it away? Garissoles continues the contrast: the text means Christ's historical act of obedience — Christ became obedient to the Father as far as the cross (Philippians 2:8) — and therefore also means Adam's historical act of breaking the command. Placeus then wonders how the learned opponent can refuse to let the Greek παρακοῆς name Adam's actual sin. The opponent adds a hedge: the word does not name actual sin peeled away from the corruption that actual sin bred in Adam. Placeus shrugs at the hedge. Key: Placeus's own published wording said παρακοῆς points to Adam's sin as such — not bare actual apart from habitual, but actual together with habitual. Does saying that amount to denying that the word names actual sin? Placeus thinks not.
pass_a.88: Why skip past that admission? Garissoles answers that either way — actual sin peeled from the corruption, or actual sin still joined to it — the designation still holds, and that is enough for the immediate-imputation brief. Placeus denies the sufficiency. If the brief is immediate imputation, mere designation is not enough. What is required is imputation of actual sin as peeled from the corruption, because on that brief the corruption is the proper penalty attached to the imputed act. Otherwise one and the same sin would be punished by itself — which Placeus will not allow, least of all when speaking of a penalty in the strict sense.
pass_a.89: Garissoles now claims a twofold harvest from verse 19. Harvest one uses the opposition's force: the way we are made sinners in Adam matches the way we are made righteous in Christ; and we are made righteous in Christ by having his righteousness imputed; so we are made sinners in Adam by having his sin imputed. Placeus grants that the closing line need not wound readers who already hold mediate imputation — yet he still calls the opening line false. The difference the leading writers already marked (and Placeus already cited) is this: sinners by inhering sin carried into us and deserving death; not righteous by inhering righteousness deserving life.
pass_a.90: Harvest two starts from the phrase that we are made sinners through Adam's disobedience. Garissoles's rule: another person's actual disobedience cannot make us sinners except by imputation, because what is personally another's cannot become ours, and cannot give us the name, unless imputation steps in. Minor: we are made sinners through Adam's actual disobedience. Conclusion: therefore by imputation. Placeus's retort treats that whole move as equivalent to refusing the propagation of inhering sin.
pass_a.91: Placeus prefers Chamier, Garissoles's own forerunner. Chamier insists one must not skip this: many were made sinners — ἁμαρτωλούς — through one person's disobedience, and Scripture uses that word for people who truly have sin against God's law inside them. Shortly after, Chamier adds that ἁμαρτωλὸς never names bare liability alone with no vice or sin present. So Paul's line about many made sinners through one disobedience meant only that Adam's sin brought it about that every human being was a real sinner in himself. Elsewhere Chamier brands as badly false the claim that Paul teaches a single numerically identical original sin in everyone; the verse about many made sinners through one disobedience stands against that claim. Same chapter: a sinner is someone who has his own sin, not someone charged with a stranger's. Again: all sinned in Adam because Adam sinned first and sin thus began in the race; yet we also sin in ourselves, because his sin made us sinners by propagating sin into us. His disobedience made us sinners in the same manner in which we are already truly sinners by our own acts — otherwise the claim that his disobedience made us sinners would be false. Another Chamier locus: we were made sinners through Adam's disobedience causally, not formally; his act efficiently causes the quality by which we are formally sinners — like a gouty father (or gout in the father) causing a gouty son without being the son's gout. Peter Martyr is then heard on the opposing side of the debate: from Paul's words that many were made sinners through one disobedience, one may argue against those who say original sin is not each person's own but only a single sin sitting in Adam that merely binds us to death and damnation. If people are called constituted sinners, they must have sin, or at least have had it. Nobody is named a sinner by a stranger's vice alone. That closes Cap. VIII VI before Caput IX.

86: VI. But perhaps that thesis will finally surface from verse 19: "As through one man's disobedience many were constituted sinners, so through one man's obedience many will be constituted righteous" (Romans 5:19). In no way. D. Garissoles argues from it in more than one form, and first thus: the Apostle in this verse is doing what he had pursued more diffusely in those earlier ones; but in this verse he plainly treats imputation; therefore the earlier verses must be understood of the same imputation. I answer the minor: in this verse the Apostle is not treating imputation; or if he is, he is not treating immediate or antecedent imputation — the only kind I deny. For if he is doing in this verse what he did in the earlier ones, where it was plain he was not treating that imputation, it follows that he is not treating that imputation in this verse either.
87: Next, he says, the Apostle could scarcely have marked the imputation of Adam's sin more clearly or forcefully than these words do, with their sharp opposition between Adam's disobedience and Christ's obedience. How then did the greatest men, expounding that verse, fail to notice that imputation in the Apostle's words — and rather reject it? But let him go on: it marks Christ's actual obedience, by which Christ became obedient to the Father unto the death of the cross (Philippians 2:8). Therefore it also marks Adam's actual disobedience, by which he violated God's command — so it is strange that the learned man denies that by the word παρακοῆς the Apostle designates Adam's actual sin. As for his addition that it does not designate actual sin cut off from the corruption that sin produced in Adam, I care little. To affirm, in Placeus's own words, that παρακοῆς signifies Adam's sin alone — not as actual cut off from habitual, but together with habitual — is that denying that the word designates Adam's actual sin?
88: Why then does he not linger on that? Because, he says, whether cut off from that corruption or joined with it, it is still understood to be designated — and that is enough for our cause. No: if you are defending the cause of immediate imputation, that is not enough. Actual sin must be imputed as cut off from the corruption, if that corruption is properly the penalty of the imputed sin. For the same sin cannot be the penalty of itself — least of all a penalty properly so called.
89: From this he thinks he can draw a double argument. First from the force of the opposition: we are constituted sinners in Adam by the same reason we are constituted righteous in Christ; but in Christ we are constituted righteous by the imputation of his righteousness; therefore in Adam we are constituted sinners by the imputation of his sin. Even though the conclusion does not harm those of us who acknowledge mediate imputation, the major premise is false. On the very point in dispute the greatest men marked a difference, as our earlier replies already showed. For we were constituted sinners by inhering sin propagated into us that deserves death; we were not constituted righteous by inhering righteousness that deserves life.
90: Next, he says, from the words "through Adam's disobedience we are constituted sinners." For we cannot be constituted sinners through another's actual disobedience except imputatively: what belongs to another personally cannot become ours, nor can we be named from it, without imputation intervening. But through Adam's actual disobedience we are constituted sinners. Therefore imputatively. What is denying the propagation of inhering sin, if this is not?
91: Hear rather his predecessor Chamier. "This too must not be omitted: through one man's disobedience many were constituted sinners — ἁμαρτωλούς; which word in the Scriptures is taken for those in whom there truly is sin contrary to God's law." And a little later: "In a word. ἁμαρτωλὸς is never said of bare guilt alone and without any vice or sin. Therefore when Paul said many were constituted sinners through one man's disobedience, he meant nothing else than that by that sin of Adam it was brought about that all human beings were truly sinners in themselves." And elsewhere: that Paul teaches original sin is numerically one in all is strikingly false. For against it stands: "Through one man's disobedience many were constituted sinners." In the same chapter: "A sinner is one who himself has his own sin, not one to whom an alien sin is imputed." Again: "In Adam we all sinned, because Adam first sinned, and from that the beginning of sin was made in all human beings; yet we also sin in ourselves, because by his sin we were constituted sinners — that is, sin was propagated from him into us. And by his disobedience we were all constituted sinners in the same way we are already truly sinners by our own; otherwise it would be false that we were constituted sinners by his disobedience." Elsewhere he says we were constituted sinners through Adam's disobedience not formally but causally, because it is the efficient cause of that quality by which we are formally sinners: "Just as," he says, "a gouty parent, or gout in the parent, is the cause of a gouty child, yet is not the child's gout." Hear also Peter Martyr arguing against them. "Here," he says, "we will note that when the Apostle says, 'Through one man's disobedience many were constituted sinners,' an argument is had from these words against those who think original sin is not each person's own, but that only one existed, and that it was in Adam, by which we are bound and obligated to death and damnation. For when they are said to be constituted sinners, they themselves must have sin, or at least have had it. For no one is called a sinner by an alien vice."
